paras: The killing of Mooney Allen was the shooting of a Black man by a crowd of armed citizens in the streets of Beaumont, Texas, on July 23, 1903, after he was accused of shooting Policeman Walter Skensbury. Pursuers fired on Allen until he fell dead, with Sheriff Landry joining the chase; one account put the crowd in the hundreds. The Associated Press story ran across the country within a week, some papers calling the killing a lynching, and two Black newspapers later listed Allen among the year's lynching victims.

According to the Associated Press dispatch from Beaumont, Allen had started that day to shoot his wife and forced a Black policeman and others who interfered to retreat. The New-York Tribune's Houston correspondent called Allen "notoriously bad" and said he had shot at a "colored policeman," who fled. Brief notices in South Carolina weeklies added that the policeman he shot had been trying to arrest him for the attack on his wife.

In the wire account, Skensbury came up, Allen covered him with a Winchester and ordered him to halt, then shot him through the side and ran. Sheriff Landry, handed a loaded revolver, set off after him, while a crowd of men, many with pistols, followed and kept up a constant fire. Allen turned down Cedar street and fell dead halfway between Pearl and Main streets.

The Tribune told a longer story: after the shooting, which it placed in the morning, the sheriff's posse captured Allen in the woods and brought him back in a hack. In front of the telegraph office Allen fired at Landry, who was trying to search him, and Landry fired back. Allen jumped from the carriage and ran down the principal street with "a pursuing mob of hundreds" behind him; when he turned and raised his revolver, he "faced a hundred guns" and fell, hit a dozen times by more than a hundred shots.

The wire called Skensbury "fatally wounded," and later briefs said Allen had killed him, but no separate report of his death or funeral was found. No report of an inquest, arrests or official inquiry into Allen's death appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch appeared on July 24 in papers from Louisville and Indianapolis to Montgomery and Richmond, and in the Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas and the Savannah Morning News the next day. Weekly news digests in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Mississippi and South Dakota reduced it to a sentence or two that ran into early August.

Some headlines led with the crime, as in the Courier-Journal's "Texas Negro Shoots a Policeman" and the Hot Springs Weekly Star's "Negro Murderer Killed." Others named the crowd: the Tribune ran "Negro Shot Down by Mob," the Montgomery Advertiser "Killed by the Crowd," and the Watertown Republican "Negro Slain by a Posse." The Atlanta Constitution printed the unchanged wire text under "Negro Lynched in Texas," and the Anderson Intelligencer reported that the man "was promptly lynched," in both cases without comment. No white paper questioned the accusation against Allen.

No news report of the killing was found in the Black press. On August 7 the Seattle Republican printed a month-by-month list under the headline "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," introduced as a "pen picture" that Russia and Turkey "might do well to emulate" and as "Uncle Sam's 1003 [1903] lynching record"; under July 23 it read "Mooney Allen, Negro, Beaumont, Tex." A near-identical list appeared in the Hartford Herald, a white Kentucky weekly, on August 12. The Chicago Broad Ax's year-end chronology for 1903 placed Allen under "Lynchings," giving the reason as "for shooting policeman."

The two original accounts differ on whether Allen was ever in custody. The Tribune's Houston telegram has him captured, escaping from a hack and turning his gun on the crowd; the AP dispatch, datelined Beaumont, has him fleeing directly after the shooting and mentions no shots by him at the pursuers. They also differ on his weapon (a Winchester or a pistol) and on how many bullets struck him (a dozen or half a dozen).

reader.title: Killing of Mooney Allen
bases: Allen, accused of shooting a policeman, was chased through the streets and shot to death by a crowd of armed citizens that the papers called a 'mob', 'crowd' or 'posse', some calling the killing a lynching (A1, A3, A19, A21).

A crowd of hundreds, many with pistols, shot Allen dead in pursuit after he was accused of shooting a policeman (A1, A3); the sheriff took part and the Tribune says Allen fired at the sheriff and turned on the crowd, so whether the killing lacked lawful color is not settled, though white and Black papers alike counted it as a lynching (A19, A21, A30, A35).

The AP dispatch from Beaumont and the Tribune's separate Houston telegram agree that Allen shot Policeman Skensbury and was pursued and shot to death by a crowd, though they differ on the details (A1, A3).

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Beaumont
accounts.gist: Allen tried to shoot his wife, held Skensbury at gunpoint with a Winchester and shot him, then ran; the sheriff and an armed crowd chased him, firing constantly, until he fell dead on Cedar street.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune special telegram from Houston
accounts.gist: After shooting the policeman in the morning Allen fled to the woods, was captured by the sheriff's posse and brought in by hack; he fired at the sheriff, jumped out, and was shot down by a mob of hundreds when he turned his revolver on it.

accounts.label: Southern weekly briefs
accounts.gist: The policeman was trying to arrest the man for attempting to shoot his wife; the man was pursued and shot, or 'promptly lynched'.

accounts.label: Black-press lynching lists
accounts.gist: Allen appears under July 23 in lists of the year's lynchings, once with the note 'for shooting policeman'; no narrative given.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text unchanged under headlines such as 'Texas Negro Shoots a Policeman' and 'Killed by the Crowd', treating Allen's guilt as fact.
The Tribune headlined 'Negro Shot Down by Mob' and spoke of a 'mob of hundreds', while calling Allen 'notoriously bad' and saying he turned his gun on the crowd.
The Atlanta Constitution headed the AP text 'Negro Lynched in Texas' and the Anderson Intelligencer said the man 'was promptly lynched', without comment.
The Hot Springs Weekly Star's headline 'Negro Murderer Killed' cast the dead man as the criminal and the killing as its end.
The Seattle Republican put Allen in a 1903 'lynching record' headed 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign', likening the United States to Russia and Turkey.
The Chicago Broad Ax listed him in a year-end chronology of lynchings, 'for shooting policeman'.
